summary: Hebrew has one present tense, and in it the verb does not change for the person (I / you / he) but for **gender and number** — four forms. אָכַל “to eat”: אוֹכֵל for a man or a masculine subject, אוֹכֶלֶת for a woman, אוֹכְלִים for men or a mixed group, אוֹכְלוֹת for women only. The person is shown only by the subject, so the pronoun is never left out: אֲנִי אוֹכֵל, אַתָּה אוֹכֵל and הוּא אוֹכֵל share one form. The present is historically a participle (בֵּינוֹנִי, “the middle form”), which is why it inflects like an adjective. One form covers “I eat” and “I am eating” — there is no progressive and no helper verb “do”. The vowels depend on the verb’s pattern (binyan, see roots and patterns): paʿal אוֹכֵל, שׁוֹתֶה; piʿel מְבַשֵּׁל. After רוֹצֶה “want” or אוֹהֵב “like”, a second verb is an infinitive with לְ־: אֲנִי רוֹצֶה לֶאֱכֹל, הִיא אוֹהֶבֶת לְבַשֵּׁל. The past and the future do have person endings; they come after the foundations (C01, C02).

blocks.title: Gender and number, not person
blocks.text: The present form tells you whether the subject is masculine or feminine, one or more — never whether it is “I”, “you” or “he”. That is why the pronoun (or a noun) must always be there: אֲנִי שׁוֹתֶה, אַתָּה שׁוֹתֶה, הוּא שׁוֹתֶה.

blocks.title: Who is “I”?
blocks.text: A woman says אֲנִי אוֹכֶלֶת, אֲנִי רוֹצָה; a man אֲנִי אוֹכֵל, אֲנִי רוֹצֶה. Speaking to a woman: אַתְּ שׁוֹתָה. A group with even one man takes the masculine plural: הֵם אוֹכְלִים.

blocks.title: One form, two meanings — and no “do”
blocks.text: הִיא שׁוֹתָה קָפֶה is “she drinks coffee” and “she is drinking coffee”. A question is the same sentence with a question mark: אַתָּה שׁוֹתֶה קָפֶה? “Do you drink coffee?”

items: Masculine or feminine? One or more?
blocks.caption: Building a present-tense sentence

blocks.title: Ask yourself
questions: Who is speaking, and to whom (man or woman)?
One person or more? Is there a man in the group?
Is there a second verb after רוֹצֶה / אוֹהֵב? → the infinitive.

askYourself: Who does it? → put the pronoun or the noun first; in the present the pronoun is never left out.
Is the subject masculine or feminine? (For אֲנִי and אַתָּה / אַתְּ it depends on who speaks and to whom.)
One or more? A mixed group → masculine plural (-ִים).
Which pattern? A root ending in ה → -ֶה / -ָה (שׁוֹתֶה, שׁוֹתָה); piʿel → מְ־ in front (מְבַשֵּׁל); otherwise like אוֹכֵל.
Is there a second verb after רוֹצֶה / אוֹהֵב? → the infinitive with לְ־: לֶאֱכֹל, לִשְׁתּוֹת, לְבַשֵּׁל.
Is it a question? → the same form, no “do”: אַתָּה אוֹכֵל?
steps: Find the subject’s gender and number.
Put the object after the verb (with אֶת when it is definite).

traps: *אֲנִי אוֹכֵל said by a woman — she says אֲנִי אוֹכֶלֶת.
*הִיא שׁוֹתֶלֶת — when the root ends in ה the feminine ends in -ָה: שׁוֹתָה, רוֹצָה, קוֹנָה.
*אוֹכֵל לֶחֶם for “I eat bread” — in the present the pronoun is required: אֲנִי אוֹכֵל לֶחֶם.
A group of women with one man is masculine: הֵם אוֹכְלִים, אֲנַחְנוּ שׁוֹתִים.
רוֹצָה “she wants” ≠ רָצְתָה “she wanted”; קוֹנָה “she buys” ≠ קָנְתָה “she bought”.
No progressive: “I am eating” is just אֲנִי אוֹכֵל — no form of הָיָה.
*רוֹצֶה אוֹכֵל — after רוֹצֶה the second verb is the infinitive: רוֹצֶה לֶאֱכֹל.

seeAlso.note: Arabic’s present (the imperfect) marks the person with prefixes and also gender and number — يَأْكُلُ, تَأْكُلُ, آكُلُ …; the Hebrew present has no person at all, only four gender-number forms.
German conjugates by person and number (ich esse, du isst, er isst …) and never by gender — the reverse of the Hebrew present.
Chinese verbs never change: 我吃, 她吃, 他们吃 — time and aspect come from other words.

notes.text: Greek verbs change for the person (τρώω, τρως, τρώει) and the pronoun can go; the Hebrew present changes for gender and number only (אוֹכֵל / אוֹכֶלֶת / אוֹכְלִים / אוֹכְלוֹת), so the pronoun must stay.
The Russian present has person endings (ем, ешь, ест) and shows gender only in the past (ел / ела); the Hebrew present is the reverse — gender and number, but no person.

Spanish endings show the person (como, comes, come), so yo can be left out; the Hebrew present shows gender and number instead, so אֲנִי must be said. There is no estar + -ndo: אֲנִי אוֹכֵל is “I eat” and “I am eating”.
English needs “do” and “am …-ing”; Hebrew has neither: אֲנִי אוֹכֵל is “I eat”, “I am eating” and, with a question mark, “do I eat?”. But the verb changes for gender: a woman says אֲנִי אוֹכֶלֶת.
Where French conjugates for the person (je mange, tu manges), the Hebrew present changes for gender and number only — a woman says אֲנִי אוֹכֶלֶת — and one form also covers “être en train de”.
German conjugates for person and number (ich esse, du isst); Hebrew for gender and number only — the pronoun shows the person.
Hindi also marks gender in the present (मैं खाता हूँ / मैं खाती हूँ), with the auxiliary showing the person; Hebrew has only the gender-and-number form (אֲנִי אוֹכֵל / אוֹכֶלֶת) and no auxiliary.
Persian verbs end in person endings (می‌خورم, می‌خوری); the Hebrew present has no person endings, but changes for gender and number.

Marathi also changes the present for the speaker’s gender (मी खातो / मी खाते); Hebrew does the same (אֲנִי אוֹכֵל / אֲנִי אוֹכֶלֶת), but uses one form for “I”, “you” and “he”, so the pronoun is needed.
The Arabic imperfect has person prefixes (آكُلُ, تَأْكُلُ, يَأْكُلُ); the Hebrew present is a participle (like Arabic آكِل) with no person marking — only gender and number.
Turkish personal endings show the person (yerim, yersin, yer); the Hebrew present shows gender and number, and the pronoun shows the person.
Japanese verbs do not change for person or gender (食べる); Hebrew verbs change for gender and number: אוֹכֵל / אוֹכֶלֶת / אוֹכְלִים / אוֹכְלוֹת. There is no ている: one form covers “eat” and “is eating”.
Korean verbs change for politeness and tense, not for the subject (먹어요); the Hebrew present changes for the subject’s gender and number.
Finnish verbs have person endings (syön, syöt, syö); the Hebrew present has none — but it has gender and number.
Hungarian verbs show person and number (eszem, eszel, eszik); the Hebrew present shows gender and number instead.
Swahili shows the person with a prefix (ninakula, unakula, anakula); the Hebrew present shows gender and number, so the pronoun is needed: אֲנִי אוֹכֵל.
Luganda puts the person in a verb prefix; the Hebrew present has no person marking at all — only gender and number — so the subject must be said.
Chinese verbs never change (我吃 / 她吃); Hebrew present verbs change for gender and number (אֲנִי אוֹכֵל / הִיא אוֹכֶלֶת). As in Chinese, one form covers “eat” and “is eating”.
Vietnamese verbs never change (tôi ăn, cô ấy ăn); Hebrew verbs change for gender and number: אֲנִי אוֹכֵל, הִיא אוֹכֶלֶת.

Inuktitut verbs carry the person and number (singular, dual, plural) of the subject — and of the object; the Hebrew present carries only the gender and number of the subject, and the object is a separate word.
